domainCoverage.synopsis: High-throughput vector search, low-latency embedding retrieval, and resilient model inference pipelines under dynamic token generation workloads.

chapters.title: Vector Embeddings, Dot Product & Cosine Similarity
chapters.summary: Vector embeddings map text, images, or code into dense fixed-length coordinate spaces where semantic proximity translates to geometric closeness, measured via cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.

chapters.title: Embedding Model Selection
chapters.summary: Embedding models map text, code, or multimodal inputs into dense (or sparse) vectors where geometric distance captures semantic similarity for RAG, search, and clustering.

chapters.title: Vector Database Indexing, HNSW Graphs & Capacity Estimation
chapters.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM outputs by indexing domain documents as dense/sparse vectors and retrieving top-k relevant chunks at query time via approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW.

chapters.title: Hybrid Vector & Keyword Search
chapters.summary: Hybrid vector search combines sparse lexical scoring (BM25) with dense semantic embeddings (HNSW/IVF) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and optional cross-encoder reranking to achieve high recall on both exact identifiers and conceptual queries.

chapters.title: RAG Retrieval Pipelines
chapters.summary: Production RAG retrieval combines semantic chunking, hybrid dense (HNSW) + sparse (BM25/SPLADE) search, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), metadata pre-filtering, and cross-encoder reranking to deliver high-precision context to LLMs.

chapters.title: Context Compression for RAG
chapters.summary: Techniques that prune, rerank, or summarize retrieved RAG chunks before LLM generation to slash token cost and TTFT while beating 'lost-in-the-middle' attention decay.

chapters.title: Deep Learning Foundations: Backpropagation, Transformers & Optimizers
chapters.summary: Modern deep learning combines reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation), parallelizable sequence modeling via scaled dot-product self-attention (Transformers), and adaptive momentum-based gradient updates (AdamW) to train multi-billion-parameter networks stably.

chapters.title: Transformer Self-Attention
chapters.summary: Self-attention lets every token dynamically weight and aggregate information from all other tokens in a sequence in parallel, replacing sequential recurrent bottlenecks with matrix multiplications over Query, Key, and Value projections.

chapters.title: Model Serving & GPU Batching
chapters.summary: Group concurrent inference requests into tensor batches on the GPU to shift workloads from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound without blowing tail latency.

chapters.title: LLM Quantization, GPTQ/AWQ & Inference Performance
chapters.summary: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.

chapters.title: Semantic Caching for LLMs
chapters.summary: Semantic LLM caching intercepts natural-language prompts, embeds them into dense vectors (e.g., 1536-dim via text-embedding-3-small), and performs an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) lookup in a vector store like Redis or Qdrant. When cosine similarity clears a strict threshold (typically 0.93–0.96), the system returns a cached completion in 20–45 ms instead of paying 1.5–6 seconds and $0.01–$0.05 per frontier model inference.

chapters.title: LLM Fine-Tuning & LoRA
chapters.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes a pretrained LLM's weights and trains tiny rank-decomposed adapter matrices, cutting fine-tuning VRAM by 3–10x while preserving base capabilities.

chapters.title: LLM Agent Tool Use
chapters.summary: LLM Agent Tool Use pairs a language model with typed JSON Schema function definitions and a runtime loop (e.g., ReAct), enabling the model to emit structured tool calls, execute deterministic code or APIs, and condition its next reasoning step on grounded observations.

chapters.title: Prompt Injection Defenses
chapters.summary: Prompt injection defense prevents untrusted user inputs or retrieved external content (RAG chunks, emails, web pages) from hijacking an LLM's control plane and triggering unauthorized tool calls or data exfiltration.

chapters.title: Prompt Engineering, LLM Reasoning & Thinking Models
chapters.summary: Systematic design of system instructions, context layout, delimiters, and constrained output schemas to make LLM behavior reliable, cache-friendly, and production-grade.

chapters.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
chapters.summary: Multi-agent orchestration coordinates specialized LLM agents—each with scoped prompts, tools, and memory—using explicit control topologies like supervisor graphs, handoff swarms, or DAG pipelines. Rather than stuffing 40 tools and conflicting instructions into one monolithic prompt, orchestration isolates responsibilities, bounds token growth, and enforces deterministic state transitions.

chapters.title: AI Agents, LangGraph & Stateful Tool Orchestration
chapters.summary: Stateful LLM agents model multi-step reasoning, tool calls, and human approvals as explicit directed cyclic graphs rather than fragile, unbounded while-loops.

chapters.title: LLM Evaluation Harnesses
chapters.summary: An automated testing and scoring pipeline that measures LLM accuracy, safety, latency, and cost across curated datasets before and after every prompt, model, or retrieval change.

chapters.title: Feature Stores for ML
chapters.summary: A feature store is a dual-plane ML data platform that computes, versions, and serves consistent features across both batch model training (offline) and low-latency real-time inference (online).

chapters.title: ML Pipeline Orchestration
chapters.summary: Coordinate multi-stage data prep, distributed training, evaluation, and deployment as idempotent, lineage-tracked DAGs rather than fragile cron scripts.

learningJourney.title: Vector Embeddings, Mathematical Spaces & Similarity
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how unstructured data maps to continuous vector spaces and how distance metrics behave on hardware.
learningJourney.explanation: Embedding models project text, images, or code into dense floating-point vectors in R^D (commonly D = 768 to 3072). Choosing between Cosine similarity, Euclidean (L2) distance, and Inner Product depends on whether vector magnitude carries signal. When vectors are L2-normalized to unit length (||v|| = 1), Euclidean squared distance reduces to 2 - 2(a · b), making Cosine, L2, and Dot Product rank-equivalent while letting CPUs compute similarity as raw AVX-512 or NEON SIMD dot products. In high dimensions, random vector distances concentrate around their mean (curse of dimensionality), so models trained with contrastive or Matryoshka losses are required to preserve meaningful angular separation.

benefits: Invariant to vector magnitude; focuses purely on semantic direction.
Reduces to a single dot product when embeddings are pre-normalized at ingest.
costs: Ignores document length or popularity signals if magnitude encodes importance.
Requires extra norm division at query time if vectors are not pre-normalized.

benefits: Preserves both magnitude and directional separation.
Natural fit for spatial clustering (k-means) and anomaly detection.
costs: Sensitive to unnormalized scale differences across heterogeneous encoders.
Higher arithmetic cost per comparison (subtractions + squaring) than raw dot product.

benefits: Fastest hardware execution via fused multiply-add (FMA) SIMD instructions.
Allows embedding models to encode prior popularity or confidence in vector norm.
costs: Unbounded score range complicates threshold-based semantic caching.
High-norm outlier vectors can dominate top-k results unfairly.

ideas.title: Unit Normalization at Ingest
ideas.description: Normalize embeddings to unit L2 norm once during ingestion so query-time cosine similarity executes as a pure SIMD dot product without square-root or division instructions.

ideas.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)
ideas.description: Models trained with MRL pack coarse semantics into early dimensions, allowing a 3072-d vector to be truncated to 512-d or 256-d for fast first-stage retrieval before full-dimension rescoring.

example.title: Pre-normalizing 1536-d embeddings for AVX-512 throughput
example.scenario: A semantic product-matching service ran cosine similarity across 200,000 candidate vectors per shard and hit CPU saturation during peak traffic.
example.reasoning: Profiling showed 32% of query CPU cycles went to computing vector norms on the fly. Pre-normalizing vectors at write time and switching the index metric to inner product enabled contiguous AVX-512 FMA dot products, cutting p95 scoring CPU time by 35% with identical top-k rankings.
example.lesson: Pre-normalize unit vectors at ingestion so query-time similarity becomes pure SIMD multiply-add.

learningJourney.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) & Vector Indexing
learningJourney.purpose: Trade bounded recall loss for sub-10ms latency and predictable RAM budgets at million-to-billion vector scale.
learningJourney.explanation: Exact K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) scans every vector in O(N * D) time, saturating DRAM bandwidth long before compute. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes eliminate exhaustive scans. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper sparse layers act as express highways and lower dense layers refine the local neighborhood in O(log N) hops, tuned via M (edges per node), efConstruction, and efSearch. Inverted File (IVF) indexes partition the space into k Voronoi cells via k-means and scan only the nearest nprobe cells. To fit billion-scale corpora in RAM, Product Quantization (PQ) splits a D-dimensional vector into M sub-vectors and encodes each to an 8-bit centroid ID—compressing a 1536-d FP32 vector (6,144 bytes) down to 96 bytes (64x compression) at the cost of slight quantization error.

benefits: High recall (97-99%) at sub-10ms p99 latency without centroid training.
Supports incremental inserts and deletes with strong query-time QPS.
costs: High RAM overhead (raw vectors plus graph adjacency lists).
Slow index build times and expensive in-memory tombstones on heavy deletes.

benefits: 10x-64x smaller memory footprint via sub-vector centroid codebooks.
Predictable linear scan over nprobe cells with high cache locality.
costs: Requires periodic k-means/codebook retraining as data distribution drifts.
Lower recall unless paired with a second-stage disk/RAM rescore of top candidates.

learningJourney.title: Hybrid Search: Dense Semantic Vectors & Sparse BM25
learningJourney.purpose: Combine conceptual semantic recall with exact lexical precision using calibrated rank fusion.
learningJourney.explanation: Dense bi-encoder embeddings compress entire passages into a single fixed-width vector, which blurs rare tokens, exact SKUs, stack traces, and invoice IDs. Sparse lexical algorithms like BM25 score exact term matches using saturated term frequency (k1) and document-length normalization (b) weighted by Inverse Document Frequency (IDF), while neural sparse models like SPLADE expand documents into learned vocabulary weights. Because BM25 scores are unbounded positive floats and cosine scores lie in [-1, 1], summing raw scores directly is unstable. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists purely by position: RRF(d) = sum(1 / (k + rank_i(d))) with k = 60, ensuring documents ranked highly by both retrievers rise deterministically.

ideas.description: Use a masked-language-model head to project passages into high-dimensional sparse vectors that capture synonyms (e.g. 'car' -> 'automobile') while remaining compatible with inverted indexes.

example.reasoning: Deployed parallel Qdrant HNSW dense retrieval and BM25 inverted-index search, merging top-100 candidates from each leg via RRF (k = 60). Exact identifier recall hit 99.4% and overall NDCG@10 improved by 42% at 18ms p95 latency.

learningJourney.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Architecture
learningJourney.purpose: Design multi-stage retrieval pipelines that ground LLM generation in fresh, access-controlled data.
learningJourney.explanation: Naive RAG—embed a raw user query, fetch top-k chunks, and stuff them into a prompt—fails on ambiguous phrasing, multi-hop questions, and strict ACL filtering. Short user questions occupy a different region of embedding space than long declarative answers; HyDE bridges this gap by generating a hypothetical answer first and embedding that passage. Multi-query expansion and sub-query decomposition split compound requests into parallel retrievals. Equally critical is enforcing tenant and document permissions via metadata pre-filtering inside the index rather than post-filtering, which can return zero results when an authorized subset is small.

learningJourney.title: Chunking Strategies, Context Compression & Reranking
learningJourney.purpose: Maximize signal-to-noise ratio in the LLM context window through smart chunking and cross-encoder reranking.
learningJourney.explanation: Bi-encoder embeddings encode queries and documents independently in O(1) vector lookups, losing fine-grained token-to-token interactions. Cross-encoders concatenate (query, chunk) and run full self-attention across both, producing dramatically more accurate relevance scores at O((L_q + L_d)^2) compute cost—making them ideal as a second-stage filter over the top 50–100 hybrid hits. Chunking faces a core tension: small chunks (128–256 tokens) yield sharp embeddings, while LLMs need surrounding context (1024+ tokens) to reason accurately. Parent-child indexing resolves this by indexing small child chunks while returning their parent section to the generator, and placing the highest-ranked chunks at the start and end of the prompt mitigates the 'Lost in the Middle' attention decay.
caveats: Cross-encoder latency scales linearly with candidate count K; cap reranking to top 30-50 chunks or run on dedicated GPU batching.
Fixed-character chunking splits tables, code blocks, and sentences mid-thought; use structure-aware or recursive splitters.
Stuffing 30+ chunks into long-context windows inflates TTFT (Time to First Token) quadratically during prefill and degrades accuracy.

ideas.title: Parent-Child Retrieval

example.title: Eliminating missed clauses in 100-page legal contract QA
example.scenario: A legal assistant injected top-30 500-token chunks into the prompt, yet the LLM repeatedly missed exception clauses placed in chunks 12 through 22.

learningJourney.title: Deep Learning Foundations & GPU Tensor Hardware
learningJourney.purpose: Understand tensor memory layouts, autograd graphs, Tensor Cores, and the GPU Roofline model.
learningJourney.explanation: Deep learning workloads are governed by GPU hardware physics. Tensors are N-dimensional views over contiguous 1D memory buffers indexed via shape and stride metadata; non-contiguous transposes must be materialized before coalesced GPU memory reads. Training builds a dynamic or static computation graph for reverse-mode automatic differentiation (autograd), storing intermediate activations in VRAM unless activation checkpointing recomputes them on the fly. On modern GPUs, Tensor Cores execute warp-level Matrix Multiply-Accumulate (MMA) in FP16, BF16, or FP8 at hundreds of teraflops. By the Roofline model, arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved from HBM) determines whether an operation is compute-bound (LLM prompt prefill, large GEMMs) or memory-bandwidth-bound (token-by-token LLM decode, elementwise activations).

ideas.title: Prefill vs. Decode Roofline Split
ideas.description: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large matrix-matrix multiplications (compute-bound), whereas autoregressive decode processes 1 token per sequence per step (HBM bandwidth-bound).

ideas.title: BF16 & FP8 Precision Trade-offs
ideas.description: BF16 preserves FP32's 8-bit exponent range to prevent training gradient underflow, while FP8 cuts weight and KV-cache HBM traffic in half during inference.

example.title: Breaking the HBM bandwidth wall in 70B decode

example.reasoning: Each decode step streamed ~140 GB of weights from HBM for a single token per request. Quantizing weights to FP8 (halving HBM bytes per token) and enabling continuous batching raised arithmetic intensity across concurrent sequences, boosting decode tokens/sec by 2.4x.
example.lesson: Autoregressive LLM decode is gated by HBM memory bandwidth; increase batching or quantize weights to raise arithmetic intensity.

reflectionQuestions: Which phase of your inference pipeline is compute-bound (TTFT/prefill) vs. HBM bandwidth-bound (ITL/decode)?
When does kernel fusion (e.g., `torch.compile` / Triton) eliminate intermediate HBM round-trips for elementwise ops?

learningJourney.title: Transformer Architecture & Attention Physics
learningJourney.purpose: Master attention math, FlashAttention SRAM tiling, GQA/MQA, RoPE, and PagedAttention KV-caching.
learningJourney.explanation: Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where scaling by sqrt(d_k) keeps dot-product variance near 1 so softmax gradients do not vanish. Materializing the N x N attention matrix in HBM scales quadratically in memory and bandwidth; FlashAttention tiles Q, K, and V blocks into fast on-chip GPU SRAM and computes softmax incrementally via online rescaling, keeping memory O(N). During autoregressive generation, caching past K and V tensors avoids recomputing the prefix, but KV-cache size (2 * layers * kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_param * seq_len) quickly dominates VRAM. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares K/V heads across groups of Q heads to shrink KV-cache traffic, RoPE encodes relative token positions via 2D rotations, and PagedAttention allocates KV-cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks to eliminate fragmentation.

ideas.title: FlashAttention Online Softmax Tiling
ideas.description: Fuse QK^T, masking, softmax, and V multiplication inside GPU SRAM tiles so the quadratic N x N score matrix is never written to slow HBM.

ideas.title: PagedAttention Virtual KV Blocks
ideas.description: Manage KV-cache like OS virtual memory pages so sequences grow dynamically without reserving contiguous max-context VRAM buffers.

example.lesson: KV-cache memory management—not raw FLOPs—determines concurrent LLM serving capacity.
